summary: Defines a set of reserved anycast addresses within each IPv6 subnet prefix, and lists their initial allocation. These addresses let a node reach a router or service on a subnet without knowing which specific one.

plainLanguage.summary: An anycast address is one address that several machines answer to, and the network sends each packet to the nearest of them. This document reserves the top 128 addresses of every IPv6 subnet for such services, so a router or a home agent can be reached at a known address without anyone having to configure it.

subtitle: Sets aside a block of addresses in every IPv6 subnet so a node can reach a router or service without knowing which one.

tldr.problem: IPv6 already defines one reserved anycast address, the Subnet-Router anycast address for routers on a subnet, but it leaves other services to pick their own anycast addresses from the unicast space.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves the highest 128 interface identifier values of every subnet prefix for subnet anycast addresses. Each one is built from a 7-bit anycast identifier, with the remaining high bits of the interface identifier set to ones.
tldr.outcome: A subnet can now offer well-known services at fixed addresses, such as the Mobile IPv6 Home-Agents anycast address with identifier 126. New identifiers are assigned centrally, in descending numerical order, with IESG approval.

today: RFC 2526 is a Proposed Standard published in March 1999. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Anycast Addresses Are For
sections.content:
IPv6 defines an anycast address as an address assigned to one or more network interfaces, typically on different nodes, with the property that a packet sent to it is routed to the nearest interface having that address, according to the routing protocols' measure of distance.

The uses of anycast addresses are still evolving, but the RFC names two. An anycast address may let nodes access one of a collection of servers providing a well-known service, without manual configuration in each node of the list of servers. Or an anycast address may be used in a source route to force routing through a specific Internet service provider, without limiting routing to a single specific router that provides access to that provider.

IPv6 already defines a required Subnet-Router anycast address for all routers within a subnet prefix, and allows additional anycast addresses to be taken from the unicast address space. This document defines a further set of reserved anycast addresses within each subnet prefix and lists their initial allocation.
sections.plainLanguage: Several machines can share one address. The network sends the packet to the closest one, so a service can be spread out without the clients knowing where it runs.

sections.title: How the Addresses Are Built
sections.content:
Within each subnet, the highest 128 interface identifier values are reserved for assignment as subnet anycast addresses. The subnet prefix consists of all fields of the IPv6 address except the interface identifier field.

For IPv6 address types required to have 64-bit interface identifiers in EUI-64 format, currently those with format prefixes 001 through 111 except for multicast addresses, the reserved subnet anycast address is a 64-bit subnet prefix followed by 57 one bits and a 7-bit anycast identifier. The universal/local bit of the interface identifier MUST be set to 0, to indicate that the interface identifier is not globally unique. For other address types the interface identifier is not in EUI-64 format and may be other than 64 bits long: the address is a subnet prefix of n bits, then 121-n one bits, then the 7-bit anycast identifier.

The reserved addresses are allocated from the IPv6 unicast address space, are reserved on all links with all subnet prefixes, and MUST NOT be used for unicast addresses assigned to any interface.

The highest addresses were chosen rather than the lowest ones to avoid conflicting with existing official and unofficial uses of low-numbered addresses in a subnet, such as the ends of a point-to-point link, tunnel endpoints, manually configured unicast addresses used when a hardware token is not available, and manually configured static addresses for the routers on a link. Reserving only 128 values for anycast identifiers, rather than perhaps 256, means the minimum possible size of an interface identifier is 8 bits, which keeps the division between subnet prefix and interface identifier byte-aligned.
sections.plainLanguage: Each reserved address ends with a 7-bit number, and the bits above that number are all ones. The subnet prefix is copied unchanged from the subnet. Taking the top of the range keeps clear of addresses people already use for point-to-point links and routers.

sections.title: The Initial Anycast Identifiers
sections.content:
Three entries are defined at the start. Anycast identifier 127, hexadecimal 7F, is reserved. Anycast identifier 126, hexadecimal 7E, is the Mobile IPv6 Home-Agents anycast address. Identifiers 0 through 125, hexadecimal 00 through 7D, are reserved.

Additional anycast identifiers are expected to be defined in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Only one identifier has a job so far: number 126 points at the Mobile IPv6 home agents of a subnet. The rest are held back.

sections.title: Worked Example: The Home Agents Address
sections.content:
The Mobile IPv6 Home-Agents subnet anycast address uses the 7-bit anycast identifier 126, hexadecimal 7E. For address types whose interface identifiers are 64 bits long and in EUI-64 format, the address is the 64-bit subnet prefix followed by the interface identifier shown here, where the first bit is the universal/local bit and the last seven bits are the anycast identifier:

1111110111111111 1111111111111111 1111111111111111 1111111111111110

For other address types the interface identifier may be other than 64 bits long and is not in EUI-64 format. Assuming a 64-bit interface identifier for comparison, the address is the same subnet prefix followed by this interface identifier, in which only the last seven bits carry the anycast identifier:

1111111111111111 1111111111111111 1111111111111111 1111111111111110
sections.plainLanguage: To build the home agents address, copy the subnet prefix and finish with a fixed 64-bit pattern whose last seven bits are 1101110, which is 126 in binary.

sections.title: How New Identifiers Are Assigned
sections.content:
This document defines a set of reserved subnet anycast addresses based on a set of anycast identifiers within each subnet prefix in the IPv6 unicast address space. As future needs arise, new anycast identifiers may be defined.

Such anycast identifiers MUST be reserved within all subnet prefixes, so assigning them requires centralized administration. New values SHOULD be assigned in descending numerical order, and are expected to be assigned only with IESG approval.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the identifiers must be reserved everywhere, only the IETF can hand out new ones, and it hands them out from the top of the range downwards.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The use of any type of reserved anycast addresses poses a security concern only in allowing potential attackers a well-known address to attack. By designating certain services to be located at specific reserved anycast addresses, an attacker may more profitably focus an attack against such a specific service.

Any such attack is best dealt with in each service that uses a reserved anycast address. RFC 1546, which originally proposed the idea of anycasting in IP, also points out a number of security considerations with the use of anycasting in general.
sections.plainLanguage: A well-known address is a fixed target. Each service that uses one is responsible for defending itself, and the RFC points to RFC 1546 for the general questions.
